overview: An undated list of papers for State Department file 894.6359 summarizes correspondence concerning Japan’s procurement and production of base metals and strategic materials, particularly aluminum, magnesium, bauxite, and tungsten concentrates. The entries report rising bauxite shipments from the Netherlands East Indies to Japan, a Mitsubishi representative’s attempt to purchase tungsten in Buenos Aires at an unusually high price, and Japanese purchasing activity reported through correspondents in Philadelphia, Argentina, and Mexico. Although the underlying telegrams and letters are not present in this OCR extract, the list provides a compact guide to the file’s international commercial and diplomatic connections, apparently chiefly during 1941.

subfiles.title: List of papers concerning Japanese base-metal procurement
subfiles.about: An archival contents sheet indexes telegrams and correspondence about Japan’s aluminum, magnesium, bauxite, tungsten, and strategic-material purchases.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records a May 1 telegram from Grew concerning the aluminum and magnesium industries of the Japanese Empire and the sharp increase in Japan’s bauxite quota from the Netherlands East Indies. It also notes that Nishizawa, manager of Mitsubishi’s Buenos Aires branch, offered a substantially higher price for tungsten concentrates. Further entries identify September and October correspondence involving Charles Lyon Chandler and Argentina, as well as a June 30 report from Daniels in Mexico enclosing information from a commercial attaché on proposed Japanese purchases of strategic materials.

interest: This page is useful as a roadmap to a dispersed body of economic-intelligence correspondence and reveals the worldwide reach of Japanese strategic-material procurement before the Pacific War. Especially notable are the quantitative comparison of bauxite shipments in 1939–1940 and the doubled monthly quota for 1941, alongside evidence of aggressive Mitsubishi purchasing in Buenos Aires. The index also links reporting from Tokyo, Philadelphia, Argentina, and Mexico, making it valuable for tracing how U.S. diplomats and commercial contacts monitored Japan’s access to essential industrial resources.
